anchor: O talk not to me of a name great in story
note: Story: here, history or tradition. A name great in story means a famous name.

anchor: The days of our youth are the days of our glory
note: The speaker says youth’s glory outweighs the fame of a name in history.

anchor: And the myrtle and ivy of sweet two-and-twenty
note: Myrtle: an evergreen shrub sacred to Venus, goddess of love. Ivy: a clinging evergreen vine.

anchor: Are worth all your laurels
note: Laurels: a wreath of laurel leaves, the ancient prize for victors and poets.

anchor: What are garlands and crowns to the brow that is wrinkled?
note: Garlands and crowns: wreaths of honor. A wrinkled brow can no longer enjoy them.

anchor: Then away with all such from the head that is hoary
note: Hoary: gray or white with age.

anchor: What care I for the wreaths that can only give glory?
note: Wreaths: crowns of leaves given as honors.

anchor: O Fame!—if I e’er took delight in thy praises
note: Fame is addressed as a person.

anchor: ’Twas less for the sake of thy high-sounding phrases
note: He valued fame less for its praise than for what it meant to his beloved.

anchor: There chiefly I sought thee, there only I found thee
note: He found fame’s true value only in her eyes.

anchor: There be none of Beauty’s daughters
note: Be: are, an old plural form.

anchor: With a magic like Thee
note: Beauty’s daughters are beautiful women, none with her magic.

anchor: And like music on the waters
note: The speaker compares her voice to music heard over the sea.

anchor: The charmed ocean’s pausing
note: Charmed: held spellbound, as if by magic.

anchor: The waves lie still and gleaming
note: The sea becomes calm and shining as the music sounds.

anchor: And the lull’d winds seem dreaming
note: Lull’d: soothed to quiet, made calm and still.

anchor: And the midnight moon is weaving
note: The moon weaves a chain of light across the water.

anchor: To listen and adore thee
note: Adore: to love deeply, to worship.

anchor: She walks in beauty, like the night
note: The poem compares a woman to a clear, starry night.

anchor: Of cloudless climes and starry skies
note: Climes: regions or climates. Her beauty is like a clear starry night.

anchor: Meets in her aspect and her eyes
note: Aspect: the look of a face, its expression.

anchor: Thus mellow’d to that tender light
note: Mellow’d: softened and ripened, made gentle in tone.

anchor: Which heaven to gaudy day denies
note: Gaudy: too bright and showy.

anchor: One shade the more, one ray the less
note: The balance of shade and light in her is perfect, so even a small change would spoil it.

anchor: Had half impair’d the nameless grace
note: Impair’d: damaged, made less perfect.

anchor: Which waves in every raven tress
note: Raven: glossy black, like the bird. Tress: a lock of hair.

anchor: The smiles that win, the tints that glow
note: Tints: shades of color, here in her face.

anchor: When we two parted
note: A poem of secret love ended, whose sorrow he cannot speak of.

anchor: Half broken-hearted
note: Broken-hearted: crushed by grief. The two lovers part in sorrow.

anchor: To sever for years
note: Sever: to separate. The lovers will be apart for years.

anchor: The dew of the morning
note: Sunk chill on my brow: the cold dew felt like a warning of grief to come.

anchor: Thy vows are all broken
note: Vows: solemn promises. Her promises have been broken.

anchor: A knell to mine ear
note: Knell: the sound of a bell rung slowly for a death.

anchor: Long, long shall I rue thee
note: Rue: to feel sorrow or regret about.

anchor: That thy heart could forget
note: He grieves in silence that she could forget him.

anchor: Elegy on Thyrza
note: An elegy is a poem of mourning. Thyrza is the name Byron gave the dead woman he mourns.

anchor: As aught of mortal birth
note: Aught: anything. Mortal: subject to death.

anchor: Too soon return’d to Earth
note: She died young, and her body has gone back to the earth.

anchor: There is an eye which could not brook
note: Brook: to put up with, to endure.

anchor: Nor gaze upon the spot
note: He will not even look at where she is buried.

anchor: ’Tis Nothing that I loved so well
note: He wants no tombstone to remind him that the thing he loved is now nothing.

anchor: As fervently as thou
note: Fervently: with intense feeling. His love lasted to the end.

anchor: Nor falsehood disavow
note: Disavow: to deny, to refuse to acknowledge.

anchor: the storm that lours
note: Lours: frowns, darkens threateningly, as a storm does.

anchor: I envy now too much to weep
note: He envies the dead their peaceful sleep too much to weep.

anchor: Nor need I to repine
note: Repine: to complain, to feel discontent.

anchor: Though by no hand untimely snatch’d
note: Untimely: too soon. Even without early death, the flower’s leaves would drop.

anchor: Extinguish’d, not decay’d
note: She died while still lovely rather than fading slowly.

anchor: As stars that shoot along the sky
note: Shooting stars shine most brightly as they fall.

anchor: One vigil o’er thy bed
note: Vigil: a period of watching or staying awake beside someone.

anchor: To gaze, how fondly! on thy face
note: Fondly: with great affection. He wishes he had watched over her.

anchor: Uphold thy drooping head
note: He wishes to have held her head up in her last hours.

anchor: And more thy buried love endears
note: Endears: makes dear. Her love is dearer for being buried.

anchor: Eternal Spirit of the chainless Mind!
note: Chillon is a castle on Lake Geneva. François Bonnivard was imprisoned in its dungeon by the Duke of Savoy for defending his city’s liberty.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 209, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Brightest in dungeons, Liberty, thou art
note: Dungeons: underground prison cells. Liberty shines most in such places.

anchor: The heart which love of Thee alone can bind
note: Only love of liberty can bind the heart.

anchor: To fetters, and the damp vault’s dayless gloom
note: Fetters: chains for the feet. Vault: an underground chamber.

anchor: Their country conquers with their martyrdom
note: Martyrdom: suffering or death for one’s beliefs.

anchor: And thy sad floor an altar
note: Byron treats the floor of the dungeon as an altar to liberty.

anchor: Until his very steps have left a trace
note: A prisoner’s long pacing has worn a trace into the stone.

anchor: Worn as if thy cold pavement were a sod, By Bonnivard!
note: Bonnivard was a Genevan who fought the tyranny of Piedmont in the 1500s. Byron says his footsteps wore marks in the dungeon floor.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 209, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: For they appeal from tyranny to God
note: Tyranny: cruel and unjust rule.

anchor: On thee shall press no ponderous tomb
note: Ponderous: heavy and weighty, hard to lift.
